extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime politics, military accountability, and labor/industrial disputes
extracted.subtask_description: A mainstream AP news article reporting on congressional hearings about Pearl Harbor, Marshall's testimony, related military/intelligence judgments, and concurrent labor/industrial disputes. It is a factual news dispatch intended for a broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt act justifies preemptive attack
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance of Japanese warships (or a flight of foreign planes) in Hawaiian waters or over Hawaii would have been 'an overt act' and 'would have justified bombing' or other military response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context given: if warships were sighted beyond restricted waters but within range of bombers, or foreign planes flew over Hawaii, those would count as overt acts that could justify American bombers sinking enemy ships or attacking. The article quotes Marshall and witnesses discussing these thresholds as bases for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nov. 27 message did not commit commanders to jeopardize defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The November 27 message expressed the desire that Japan make the first overt act but 'specifically told the overseas commanders they were not committed to a course of action which would "jeopardize your defense."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a constraint on commanders' discretion: they could act in response to an overt act but were not authorized to take measures that would endanger their own defensive posture. Used as explanatory context for commanders' expected behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercepted diplomatic/military signals as indicators of imminent hostilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourteen-part Japanese message (combined with timed delivery instructions) was described by some witnesses as 'a proof that war was near' and thus a tip that hostile action was imminent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that intercepted/decoded diplomatic communications and combined messages were treated by officials as evidence pointing to imminent hostilities; timing and content (e.g., delivery at a given hour) contribute to that assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command responsibility and expectation of compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a command is given to a high officer, 'you expect it to be carried out.' Marshall asserted that Gen. Short 'was given an alert order' and that command responsibility implies expectation of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses an accountability standard: issuing an order creates an expectation the subordinate will implement it; failures to execute raise questions of responsibility and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication security matters for transmitting warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Marshall said he did not telephone Short because he 'feared the Japanese would intercept a telephone message'; commercial facilities were used but did not reach Short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of communication channel affects likelihood of successful warning and operational security; e.g., sensitive warnings may be withheld from insecure channels to avoid enemy interception, but that can prevent timely receipt by recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of codebreaking is vital to national security
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a 'terrible tragedy' that 'the secrets of breaking the Japanese code have been made public,' indicating that disclosure of signals intelligence undermines operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handling of intelligence and codebreaking must prioritize secrecy; leaks or public disclosure can critically damage wartime intelligence capabilities and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of naval allocation for strategic defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Marshall and Stark criticized proposals that assigned British naval forces largely to escort and patrol duties and left primary defense of the Malay barrier to U.S. and Dutch forces, calling the British contribution a 'small part' and 'insufficient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective defense of a strategic position requires adequate allocation of offensive and defensive naval assets; assigning forces only to distant escorts/patrols may be deemed inadequate for claimed vital positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined military action requires political agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The memorandum argued 'our collective military strength can only be developed fully if our governments agree to act together,' implying that committing to combined operations needs explicit governmental agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military planning for coalition/combined operations must be backed by political commitments; absence of such agreements undermines ability to develop integrated strategy and allocate forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fact-finding and compulsory cooling-off to avert major strikes
rubrics_metrics.description: President Truman requested Congress provide fact-finding boards and a compulsory 30-day cooling-off period as measures to check industrial strife (e.g., to avert a threatened steel strike).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy rubric for labor disputes: establish formal fact-finding, impose temporary cooling-off periods, and use conciliators to delay or prevent strikes that could disrupt reconversion to peacetime production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening contract bargaining upon change in national wage policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The union contended that a contract clause permitting reopening 'for a general wage increase upon a change in national wage policy' meant the union was free to bargain if such a national change occurred; the War Labor Board recognized this right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of labor contracts: explicit or implied clauses tied to national wage policy can justify reopening bargaining; administrative recognition (e.g., War Labor Board) supports that right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government economic controls to check postwar inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials urged restoring priorities, reimposing ceilings on certain goods, and extending price control authority to combat postwar inflation pressure and avoid speculative hoarding or price surges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy measures recommended include selective price ceilings, priority controls, and continued regulatory mechanisms during reconversion to stabilize prices and supply; these are framed as necessary to avoid inflationary 'psychology' and supply distortions.
